findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned disposer
findings.body: After a caller invokes the returned cleanup function, subsequent socket messages still invoke the retired handler. Repeated attach/dispose cycles therefore retain closures and produce duplicate message processing, breaking the existing teardown contract.

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned disposer
findings.body:
Calling the cleanup function no longer unsubscribes the handler. Any `"message"` emitted afterward still invokes stale handlers, causing post-disposal state updates and accumulating duplicate listeners across attach/cleanup cycles.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned disposer
findings.body:
Any consumer that invokes the returned cleanup function and later receives a `"message"` will still execute the handler. Repeated attach/cleanup cycles also accumulate listeners, breaking the existing teardown contract and potentially causing duplicate processing and leaks.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore message-handler detachment in the cleanup callback
findings.body:
After a caller invokes the returned cleanup during session teardown or handler replacement, later messages on the same socket still reach the retired handler. This breaks the listener revocation boundary, allowing untrusted socket messages to trigger stale authorization/session logic and causing handlers to accumulate across repeated attach/cleanup cycles.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned disposer
findings.body:
On a long-lived socket, repeated `attach()`/dispose cycles retain every handler because the disposer is now a no-op. This leaks handler closures and causes duplicate message processing that grows linearly with each cycle.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
